Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

emperor noun

also Roman emperor, Caesar

classical

Tac. Ann. 3.74 (Lewis & Short)
Suet. Galb. 6 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 179
M-O s.v. emperor

imperātor, imperātōris m.

noun, third declension

emperor; first a commander

First a commander, and the title soldiers gave a victorious general; from Augustus on a title of the emperors, and then the plain word for an emperor (Lewis & Short). Traupman and Morgan–Owens use it for any emperor, of China too (Wolff, 1726). An empress is imperātrix (Levi–Bini p. 33), a rare word in antiquity.

Other words

  • prīnceps, prīncipis m. — the emperor, the first citizen

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Tac. Ann. 1.1: nōmine prīncipis; Tac. Agr. 42.5; Traupman 179

    The title Augustus chose: he took the state, worn out by civil war, under his power nōmine prīncipis (Tac. Ann. 1.1). The usual word for the emperor in Tacitus and Pliny; Lewis & Short call this sense poetic and post-Augustan.

  • Caesar, Caesaris m. — Caesar, the emperor

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Mart. 14.73.2; M-O s.v. emperor

    Julius Caesar’s family name, borne by every emperor after him (Lewis & Short); Morgan–Owens gives it for the emperors who claimed the Roman succession.

Examples

  • posse etiam sub malīs prīncipibus magnōs virōs esse

    that there can be great men even under bad emperorsTac. Agr. 42.5

  • psittacus ā vōbīs aliōrum nōmina discam: hoc didicī per mē dīcere «Caesar, havē»

    I, the parrot, shall learn other names from you; this I learned to say by myself: “Hail, Caesar!”Mart. 14.73

See also empire, king, palace.
